en: The Philippine eagle, our national bird, has a distinctive crest of dark brown feathers and hunts monkeys in the canopy of Mindanao's tropical rainforests.
The sampaguita, our national flower, blooms with fragrant white petals and grows abundantly in local gardens and along fences across the Philippine archipelago.
The ancient Ifugao rice terraces demonstrate indigenous engineering by carving stepped agricultural fields into the steep mountain slopes of the Cordilleras to capture rainwater.
During the Pahiyas Festival, locals decorate their homes with colorful kiping, which are leaf-shaped decorations made by dyeing and drying flattened rice grains.
National Scientist Ramon Barba discovered how to induce mango flowering by smoldering charcoal under the trees, allowing farmers to harvest fruit year-round.
The Philippine Constitution mandates the state and its citizens to protect and advance the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology.
The Philippine pearl, specifically the South Sea pearl produced by the Pinctada maxima oyster in the waters of Palawan, is our national gem.
The Tboli people weave the traditional tnalak cloth using abaca fibers that they extract, dry, and dye with natural colors from local roots and leaves.
National Scientist Angel Alcala pioneered the establishment of marine sanctuaries in the Philippines to protect coral reefs and restore local fish populations.
The narra, our national tree, is a large hardwood species that drops its leaflets during the dry season and produces clusters of yellow flowers.
The carabao, our national animal, is a domesticated swamp buffalo that thrives in muddy environments and helps farmers plow wet rice paddies.
The Ecological Solid Waste Management Act requires every Filipino household to segregate their biodegradable, non-biodegradable, and recyclable trash at the source.
